neck-isometric-extension.name: Neck Isometric — Extension
neck-isometric-extension.execution: Sit or stand tall. Place both hands behind the head.',. Press the head backward into the hands — maximum isometric force.',. The hands resist — neither head nor hands move.',. Hold for the time prescribed on the workout card. Release.',. Repeat for the prescribed number of sets.',. Build hold duration and pressure progressively over weeks.',.
neck-isometric-extension.why: Neck strength is a critical injury-prevention factor in hockey — a stronger neck reduces the risk of concussion by attenuating the rotational head acceleration that occurs during impacts. Every pound of neck strength reduces head acceleration by roughly 5% in an impact. Isometric extension strengthens the posterior neck and upper trapezius directly.
neck-isometric-extension.transfer: Neck extension strength reduces whiplash injury risk during hits and falls. Concussion-prevention research consistently identifies neck strength as a modifiable risk factor. Modify it.
neck-isometric-extension.cues: "Lie face down" · "Lift head 1 inch off floor and hold. Or push palm against back of head and resist. Hold for the time prescribed on the workout card."
neck-isometric-extension.mistakes: Holding the breath — breathe steadily during the isometric hold.',. Too much force too soon — build neck strength gradually.',. Skipping it because it feels awkward — neck training prevents serious injury.',. Only doing extension — train all four directions equally.',.
neck-isometric-extension.progression: Progress: Neck harness with weight plates — progressive overload for serious neck strength.', | Regress: Very light pressure holds — begin with minimal force and build gradually.',

neck-isometric-flexion.name: Neck Isometric — Flexion
neck-isometric-flexion.execution: Sit or stand tall, spine neutral. Place one or both hands on your forehead. Press the head FORWARD into the hands — maximum isometric force. Hands resist — no movement occurs. Hold for the time prescribed on the workout card. Release and repeat for the prescribed number of sets. Progress by increasing hold duration before increasing force.
neck-isometric-flexion.why: The deep neck flexors (longus colli, longus capitis) are the most important concussion-mitigating muscles — they pre-tense before impact and reduce the head's free rotational acceleration. Most hockey players have chronically weak flexors from the forward-head skating posture, leaving them more vulnerable to head injuries. Isometric flexion directly targets these muscles and is the fastest way to build protective neck stiffness.
neck-isometric-flexion.transfer: Neck strength is a modifiable concussion risk factor. This is THE most-skipped hockey prehab exercise. Cheap weekly insurance. Most hockey players ignore neck work until they get hit. Don't wait.
neck-isometric-flexion.cues: "Lie on back. Lift head 1 inch off floor and hold under tension. Or push palm against forehead — push back against your hand. Hold for the time prescribed on the workout card."
neck-isometric-flexion.mistakes: Jutting the chin forward — keep the chin slightly tucked throughout. Holding the breath — breathe steadily during the hold. Skipping this in favour of extension only — all four directions equally important. Too aggressive too soon — neck training must be progressive.
neck-isometric-flexion.progression: Progress: Weighted flexion with a neck harness — progressive overload for serious neck development. | Regress: Very light fingertip pressure holds — start minimal and build over weeks.

neck-isometric-lateral.name: Neck Isometric — Lateral
neck-isometric-lateral.execution: Sit or stand tall. Place one hand against the side of the head above the ear. Press the head sideways into the hand — maximum isometric force. Hand resists — no movement. Hold for the time prescribed on the workout card. Release and repeat each side for the prescribed number of sets. Both left and right equally — check which side is weaker and give it extra attention. Progress hold duration before increasing force.
neck-isometric-lateral.why: Lateral neck strength resists the sideways head snap that occurs during shoulder checks and board impacts — the most common mechanism of hockey concussion. Building lateral isometric strength in both directions creates a neck that stiffens reflexively before contact, dramatically reducing the rotational brain movement that causes concussive injury. This is the most neglected yet most important neck training direction for hockey players.
neck-isometric-lateral.transfer: Lateral neck strength prevents the rotational concussion mechanism — most hockey concussions involve lateral or rotational forces. Standard hockey programming oversight: most miss neck work entirely. Be the exception.
neck-isometric-lateral.cues: "Push palm against side of head. Resist without letting head move. Hold each side for the time prescribed on the workout card."
neck-isometric-lateral.mistakes: Shrugging the shoulder up instead of pressing with the neck — isolate the neck. Only training one direction — dominant-side impacts are unpredictable in hockey. Neglecting the weaker side — imbalance increases injury risk on that side. Rushing through it — neck training requires patience and progressive load.
neck-isometric-lateral.progression: Progress: Band-resisted lateral neck flexion — adds dynamic resistance for stronger athletes. | Regress: Gentle self-massage first to reduce tension, then light isometric holds.

prone-hip-extension.name: Prone Hip Extension
prone-hip-extension.execution: Lie face down on the floor, arms under your forehead. Squeeze the RIGHT glute first — before any movement. Lift the right leg off the floor with the knee straight — only 10-15cm. Hold 3 seconds. You should feel it in the glute, NOT the lower back. Lower. Complete 10 reps then switch. If you feel it in the back: slow down, focus on the glute squeeze before lifting.
prone-hip-extension.why: The prone hip extension activates the gluteus maximus in isolation while the athlete is lying face-down — removing any possibility of compensating with the lower back or hamstrings. It is a pure glute firing drill used by rehabilitation specialists to re-establish the glute-first pattern that most hockey players lose from excessive sitting and skating in a forward-flexed position. When the glutes don't fire first, the lower back does — causing chronic back pain.
prone-hip-extension.transfer: Isolates glute activation in prone position — corrects glute inhibition. Useful as part of a daily glute-activation routine. Cheap, takes 3 minutes, real payoff.
prone-hip-extension.cues: "Lie face down" · "Lift leg straight up squeezing glute" · "Hold 2s" · "Lower slow"
prone-hip-extension.mistakes: Lower back doing the work instead of the glute — the lift should be small and glute-driven. No squeeze before lifting — the pre-squeeze activates the glute before the movement. Lifting too high — beyond 15cm the lower back takes over. Rushing through it — this is activation work, not conditioning.
prone-hip-extension.progression: Progress: Prone hip extension with knee bent (isolates glute even more, removes hamstring). | Regress: Simply lying prone and squeezing both glutes simultaneously — begin activation before movement.

reverse-nordic-curl.name: Reverse Nordic Curl
reverse-nordic-curl.execution: Kneel on a pad, feet anchored or held by a partner. Upright starting position. Slowly lean BACKWARD — lower the body toward the floor using quad control. The hips stay extended — this is not a sit-back. Body moves as one rigid unit. Lower as slowly as possible. Catch yourself with hands when you can no longer control. Push back up with hands and use the quads to return to upright. Start with very short range of motion. Build over weeks.
reverse-nordic-curl.why: The reverse Nordic (kneeling, leaning back under quad control) is the anterior equivalent of the Nordic curl — it eccentrically loads the rectus femoris and hip flexors in the lengthened position, building the quad strength that protects against quad strains during explosive skating accelerations. It also builds the knee extension strength needed for deeper skating stance without quad fatigue.
reverse-nordic-curl.transfer: Eccentric quad strength — prevents patellar tendinopathy and quad strains. Top hidden-gem prehab drill for hockey players. Both flexibility AND strength.
reverse-nordic-curl.cues: "Kneel" · "Body upright" · "Lean back slowly as far as possible" · "Hold" · "Return up"
reverse-nordic-curl.mistakes: Hips flexing (sitting back) — hips must stay extended. The body leans like a plank. Dropping fast — maximum slow eccentric is the entire training stimulus. Too much range too soon — start with a 20-30° lean and build. Skipping it because it's awkward — quad eccentric training is rare and valuable.
reverse-nordic-curl.progression: Progress: Increase lean angle progressively toward full floor contact over months. | Regress: Very shallow lean (10-15°) with hands ready to catch — tiny range builds the pattern safely.

serratus-anterior-push-up.name: Serratus Anterior Push-Up
serratus-anterior-push-up.execution: Start in a standard high plank or push-up position. Perform a regular push-up OR start from the top position. At full arm extension, ADD an extra push — protract the shoulder blades forward. The upper back rounds slightly and rises as the serratus fires. Lower back to the standard plank position (shoulder blades neutral). This extra protraction range at the top IS the exercise.
serratus-anterior-push-up.why: The serratus anterior (the 'boxing muscle' under the armpit) protracts and rotates the shoulder blade — critical for proper overhead mechanics and the follow-through of a shot. In hockey players, weak serratus leads to 'winging' of the shoulder blade, which is a primary cause of impingement and rotator cuff injury. The serratus push-up (push-up-plus) directly trains this often-overlooked muscle.
serratus-anterior-push-up.transfer: Prevents scapular winging and shoulder impingement from stick use. Pair with face pulls + band pull-aparts for full shoulder-health stack. Cumulative weekly insurance.
serratus-anterior-push-up.cues: "At top of push-up" · "Round upper back and push hands into floor extra"
serratus-anterior-push-up.mistakes: Skipping the protraction — without the final push-plus, this is just a push-up. Holding the breath during protraction — breathe out on the push-plus. Going too fast — the protraction at the top needs to be deliberate. Hips sagging during the movement — maintain the rigid plank throughout.
serratus-anterior-push-up.progression: Progress: Wall slide push-up-plus — arms slide up a wall, adding overhead serratus demand. | Regress: Scapular protraction from a wall — gentle push-plus standing against a wall.

single-leg-balance-reach.name: Single-Leg Balance Reach
single-leg-balance-reach.execution: Stand on one leg with a slight knee bend (10-15°). Reach the OPPOSITE leg FORWARD (anterior) — touch toe lightly, return to start. Reach the same leg OUT to the side (lateral) — touch lightly, return. Reach the same leg BEHIND you (posterior) — touch lightly, return. 3 reaches in each direction = 1 rep cycle. Switch standing leg. Slow and controlled. The standing leg's knee should stay stable — no wobbling.
single-leg-balance-reach.why: Every skating stride is a single-leg balance challenge — you're on one foot for ~70% of the stride cycle. The Star Excursion Balance Test (which this exercise is based on) is one of the most validated functional movement screens in sports medicine; reach distance in the three directions predicts lower-body injury risk. For hockey players, this exercise trains the dynamic hip stability and proprioception that turn into edge control + agility on the ice. Asymmetries between left and right are a red flag — and this drill exposes them.
single-leg-balance-reach.transfer: Every skating stride is a single-leg balance challenge. Reach drill teaches your body to stay balanced through hip movement — the exact skill that turns into edge control on the ice. Every skating stride is single-leg balance. Train the underlying skill, the on-ice version finds you.
single-leg-balance-reach.cues: "Stand on one leg" · "Slight knee bend. Reach the OTHER leg out in three directions: forward (anterior)" · "Out to the side (lateral)" · "Behind you (posterior). Touch toe lightly" · "Return to start. Slow + controlled. 3 reaches each direction = 1 rep."
single-leg-balance-reach.mistakes: Letting the standing knee cave inward — exactly the ACL-risk pattern; track it over the toes. Rushing — speed defeats the proprioceptive challenge. Slow forces stability. Touching down hard with the reaching foot — should be a light tap, not a step. Skipping the weaker side — that's where the gold is. Spend extra time on the worse leg.
single-leg-balance-reach.progression: Progress: Single-leg reach with eyes closed — removes visual input; trains pure proprioception. | Regress: Single-leg balance hold (no reach, just stand) — build the static balance first.
single-leg-balance-reach.muscles: Hip stabilizers, Glute medius, Proprioception, Ankle stability
single-leg-balance-reach.nameHint: Баланс на одной ноге с касаниями

terminal-knee-extension-tke.name: Terminal Knee Extension (TKE)
terminal-knee-extension-tke.execution: Loop a resistance band around a fixed point at knee height behind you. Place the band behind your knee. Stand with the banded leg slightly bent. Stand on the banded leg — the band pulls the knee into flexion. Drive the knee to full extension against the band — contract the quad fully. Hold lockout 2 seconds. Release slowly back to the slight bend. 10-15 reps each leg. Feel it at the inner knee (VMO).
terminal-knee-extension-tke.why: Terminal knee extension (TKE) with a band specifically targets the VMO (inner quad) and trains the full knee lockout pattern — the range most inhibited after knee injuries or surgery. In hockey players, the TKE restores proper quadriceps function at the end of the knee extension range, improves patellar tracking, and directly reduces anterior knee pain from heavy skating volume. It is the first exercise prescribed after ACL reconstruction for a reason.
terminal-knee-extension-tke.transfer: Strengthens the VMO at terminal extension — prevents patellar tracking issues. Useful for anyone with cranky knees OR anyone trying to prevent cranky knees. Cheap weekly insurance.
terminal-knee-extension-tke.cues: "Band behind knee" · "Stand on one leg" · "Fully extend knee against band resistance"
terminal-knee-extension-tke.mistakes: Not reaching full extension — the terminal range is the whole point. Going too fast — slow and deliberate for maximum VMO activation. Band too loose — should provide meaningful resistance at full extension. Skipping the 2-second hold — the hold is where VMO fires hardest.
terminal-knee-extension-tke.progression: Progress: Single-leg mini-squat (0-30° range) with band — adds load to the VMO activation pattern. | Regress: Seated quad sets (tighten quad while sitting, hold 5s) — most basic VMO activation.

wrist-pronation-supination.name: Wrist Pronation/Supination
wrist-pronation-supination.execution: Hold a light dumbbell (2-3kg) or a hammer vertically in one hand. Elbow bent at 90°, upper arm against the side. Rotate the hand to a palm-down position (pronation) — hold 1 second. Rotate back to palm-up (supination) — hold 1 second. That is one rep. Complete 12-15 each direction. The weight at the end of the dumbbell creates a lever arm. Keep the movement slow.
wrist-pronation-supination.why: Wrist pronation (turning palm down) and supination (turning palm up) train the radioulnar joint and the forearm rotators — the muscles that control the stick face angle for shot accuracy and puck handling. Hockey players who can rapidly pronate and supinate have faster stick releases and more deceptive shot mechanics. This drill also prevents the forearm tendinopathies common from repetitive unilateral rotation in skating and shooting.
wrist-pronation-supination.transfer: Prevents the forearm overuse injuries common from repeated shooting. Pair with wrist roller + wrist curls for full forearm coverage. Quiet day, real payoff for shot velocity.
wrist-pronation-supination.cues: "Dumbbell held at one end" · "Rotate palm up and down through full range"
wrist-pronation-supination.mistakes: Moving the upper arm — the upper arm must be pinned to the side. Only the forearm rotates. Going too fast — slow rotation builds more strength than momentum-driven movement. Weight too light — 2-4kg with the lever arm is already quite challenging. Only doing it in the gym — can be done anywhere with a hammer or light tool.
wrist-pronation-supination.progression: Progress: Longer implement (longer dumbbell or a thick stick) — increases lever arm demand. | Regress: No weight — practice the rotation movement with just the forearm before adding load.

90-90-hip-stretch.name: 90/90 Hip Stretch
90-90-hip-stretch.execution: Sit on the floor. Front leg: shin perpendicular to your torso, knee at 90°. Back leg: also at 90° behind you — knee pointing behind, shin pointing to the side. Sit tall on both sitting bones — don't let the back hip lift off the floor. Hold the position 60s. Then actively rotate the torso toward the front shin. Switch legs — front becomes back. Both directions equally. Add forward fold over the front shin for deeper posterior hip stretch.
90-90-hip-stretch.why: The 90-90 hip stretch targets both internal and external hip rotation in a single position — the two rotational ranges most restricted and most demanded by hockey skating. Sitting in the 90-90 position loads the hip capsule in a way no other stretch does, and the active rotations performed from this position train the hip to actively control range, not just passively stretch into it.
90-90-hip-stretch.transfer: Addresses both internal and external rotation simultaneously — crucial for goalies. If you can't sit comfortably in 90/90, your hips are limiting your skating stride. Daily work until you can.
90-90-hip-stretch.cues: "Both legs at 90°" · "Sit tall" · "Rock forward over front shin" · "Switch sides"
90-90-hip-stretch.mistakes: Back hip lifting off the floor — this reduces the internal rotation demand. Keep both hips grounded. Slumping — sit tall. Mobility requires active posture. Only doing the static hold — add the active torso rotation for hip capsule work. Rushing the switch — spend at least 60s each side before switching.
90-90-hip-stretch.progression: Progress: 90-90 with windshield wiper transition (rotate from one 90-90 to the other without hands) — full hip rotation control. | Regress: Seated figure-4 stretch — same external rotation target with less internal rotation demand.
90-90-hip-stretch.muscles: Hip External Rotators, Hip Internal Rotators, Glutes

butterfly-stretch.name: Butterfly Stretch
butterfly-stretch.execution: Sit on the floor with the soles of your feet together, knees falling out to the sides. Hold your feet with both hands and sit tall — don't let the lower back round. Gently press your knees DOWN toward the floor using your elbows. Hold breathing deeply into the stretch for the time prescribed on the workout card. For a dynamic version: slowly flap the knees up and down like butterfly wings × 20. Move your feet closer to the groin for a deeper stretch as flexibility improves.
butterfly-stretch.why: Hip adductor flexibility is the most critical and most neglected mobility factor for hockey players. The groin/adductor complex is the #1 soft-tissue injury site in hockey — accounting for 10-15% of all NHL injuries every season. The butterfly stretch directly targets these muscles in the exact position used during a wide skating stride and goalie butterfly drop.
butterfly-stretch.transfer: Essential for groin flexibility — directly improves skating stride width. Groin strain is the #2 hockey injury after concussions. This stretch is part of the prevention protocol.
butterfly-stretch.cues: "Sit tall" · "Soles together" · "Press knees toward floor gently" · "Lean forward"
butterfly-stretch.mistakes: Rounding the lower back — sit against a wall if needed to keep the spine tall. Forcing the knees down aggressively with elbows — adductor tears happen here. Gentle pressure only. Holding your breath — breathe into the stretch to deepen it. Only doing it when tight — daily is the target. Prevention requires consistency.
butterfly-stretch.progression: Progress: Weighted butterfly (light plate on knees) for deeper passive stretch. | Regress: Supine butterfly (lying on back) — gravity assists, less demand on hip flexors.

calf-wall-stretch.name: Calf Wall Stretch
calf-wall-stretch.execution: Stand facing a wall, hands on the wall for support. Step one foot back ~60-80cm, heel flat on the floor. Bend the front knee while keeping the back leg straight and back heel DOWN. Lean toward the wall until you feel a strong stretch in the back calf. Hold for the time prescribed on the workout card. Then bend the back knee slightly to target the soleus. Switch legs. Both positions (straight and bent knee) are important.
calf-wall-stretch.why: Calf and Achilles tightness restricts ankle dorsiflexion — which restricts skating knee bend — which restricts stride power and edge control. It's a chain reaction. Tight calves are also a major contributor to Achilles tendinopathy and plantar fasciitis, both of which can sideline a player for weeks. Two minutes of calf stretching daily can prevent months of missed ice time.
calf-wall-stretch.transfer: Releases calf tightness after sprints and plyometrics — protects the Achilles. Daily, especially in-season. Calves accumulate stiffness from skating; stretching prevents the lockout.
calf-wall-stretch.cues: "Hands on wall" · "One foot back. Straight leg = gastrocnemius. Bent knee = soleus. Both matter."
calf-wall-stretch.mistakes: Back heel lifting — invalidates the stretch. Heel stays on the floor. Only doing the straight-knee version — the bent-knee targets the soleus and Achilles directly. Holding for only 10 seconds — minimum 30 seconds for meaningful tissue change. Skipping it post-skate — this is when the Achilles is most vulnerable and most receptive.
calf-wall-stretch.progression: Progress: Downward dog hold — full posterior chain stretch from calves through hamstrings. | Regress: Seated towel calf stretch (towel around foot, leg straight) — fully passive.

couch-stretch.name: Couch Stretch
couch-stretch.execution: Kneel facing away from a wall or couch. Place the top of one foot against the wall. The rear shin should be as vertical as possible against the wall. Bring the other foot forward into a lunge position — front knee at 90°. Sit tall and squeeze the glute of the back leg. Do NOT arch the lower back. Hold each side breathing steadily for the time prescribed on the workout card. Progress by making the rear leg more vertical over weeks.
couch-stretch.why: The couch stretch is the most effective hip flexor and quad stretch available — targeting the rectus femoris and iliopsoas in a deep lengthened position. Chronically tight hip flexors from constant skating crouch anterior-tilt the pelvis, compressing the lumbar spine and reducing glute activation. 2 minutes per side daily restores hip extension range and immediately improves glute firing patterns.
couch-stretch.transfer: Most aggressive hip flexor stretch available — fights years of skating tightness. Pair with active glute squeezes during the hold. The glute fires, the flexor releases. That's the mechanism.
couch-stretch.cues: "Rear shin against wall" · "Front foot flat on floor" · "Drive hips forward" · "Stay tall"
couch-stretch.mistakes: Arching the lower back to get 'deeper' — this is cheating. Posterior pelvic tilt and squeeze the glute. Leaning the torso forward — you should be fully upright or even slightly leaning back. Cutting the hold short — give the tissue real time under tension to adapt. Only doing it pre-workout — pre AND post skate is ideal.
couch-stretch.progression: Progress: Elevate the front foot on a low box — increases the hip flexor stretch depth. | Regress: Kneeling hip flexor stretch (standard lunge) — same muscle, less range required.

cross-body-shoulder-stretch.name: Cross-Body Shoulder Stretch
cross-body-shoulder-stretch.execution: Stand or sit tall. Bring one arm straight across the chest at shoulder height. Use the opposite hand or forearm to gently pull the arm closer to the chest. Keep the shoulder blade DOWN — don't let it shrug up. You should feel the stretch in the back of the shoulder joint. Hold breathing steadily for the time prescribed on the workout card. Switch sides. Repeat for the prescribed sets.
cross-body-shoulder-stretch.why: The posterior shoulder capsule tightens chronically in hockey players from repeated shooting, passing, and checking motions. This tightness creates internal rotation deficit — a major contributor to shoulder impingement, labrum stress, and SLAP tears. The cross-body stretch directly targets the posterior capsule and is the #1 recommended stretch in shoulder injury prevention protocols for overhead and contact athletes.
cross-body-shoulder-stretch.transfer: Releases the rear shoulder after rows and pulling — prevents impingement. Most hockey players ignore the posterior shoulder. The injury report disagrees with that priority.
cross-body-shoulder-stretch.cues: "Pull one arm across the chest with the other" · "At shoulder height. Feel the rear delt. Hold."
cross-body-shoulder-stretch.mistakes: Shrugging the shoulder up during the stretch — pull the blade down first. Pulling aggressively — this should be a gentle, sustained stretch. Forgetting the dominant (shooting) side needs more attention. Holding less than 30 seconds — static stretch requires 30+ seconds for tissue change.
cross-body-shoulder-stretch.progression: Progress: Sleeper stretch (lying on side, internal rotation) — deeper posterior capsule target. | Regress: Door frame chest stretch — broader shoulder stretch as an easier starting point.

foam-roll-it-band.name: Foam Roll — IT Band
foam-roll-it-band.execution: Lie on your side, foam roller under the outer thigh just above the knee. Stack the legs or put the top foot on the floor for support. Roll slowly from just above the knee to just below the hip — 3-4cm per second. When you find a tender spot, PAUSE there for 5-10 seconds before moving on. Do NOT rush — slow rolling finds the adhesions that need attention. 2-3 passes per side is enough. More is not better.
foam-roll-it-band.why: IT band syndrome is one of the most common overuse injuries in hockey players — the constant lateral loading of skating compresses the IT band against the lateral femoral condyle. Foam rolling the lateral quad and TFL (the muscle that drives the IT band) reduces tissue density and improves blood flow before and after training. Note: the IT band itself can't be stretched — you're targeting the TFL and lateral quad.
foam-roll-it-band.transfer: Prevents knee pain and IT band syndrome — very common in skaters. Tight IT band = nagging outside-knee pain. Skip this and pay for it in February.
foam-roll-it-band.cues: "Side lying" · "Roller on outer thigh" · "Roll from hip to knee slowly"
foam-roll-it-band.mistakes: Rolling too fast — you're trying to find tender spots and release them, not massage quickly. Rolling directly over the knee joint — stop 2 inches above. Gritting through extreme pain — sharp pain means stop. Moderate discomfort is normal. Skipping it post-skate when the IT band is warm and most receptive.
foam-roll-it-band.progression: Progress: Lacrosse ball on the TFL (hip pocket area) — more targeted pressure. | Regress: Roller with hands on floor for support — reduces pressure if too intense.

foam-roll-quads.name: Foam Roll — Quads
foam-roll-quads.execution: Lie face down, foam roller under the front of one thigh just above the knee. Support yourself on your forearms. Roll slowly from just above the knee to just below the hip crease. Pause and hold on any tender spot for 5-10 seconds. Rotate the leg inward and outward to hit different quad heads. 60-90 seconds per leg is sufficient.
foam-roll-quads.why: The quadriceps are the most-loaded muscle group in hockey — every stride, stop, and explosive push taxes them heavily. Foam rolling the quads before training increases tissue extensibility, reduces stiffness, and allows deeper knee bend in squats and skating. Post-training rolling reduces delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) and speeds recovery between sessions — critical in a heavy game schedule.
foam-roll-quads.transfer: Releases quad tightness from skating — reduces patellar tendon stress. Pair with couch stretch for full quad + hip flexor recovery. Post-game, post-practice — daily.
foam-roll-quads.cues: "Lie face down" · "Roller under thighs" · "Roll slowly from hip to above knee" · "Pause on tight spots"
foam-roll-quads.mistakes: Rolling too fast over tender spots — pause and breathe through it. Starting at the hip instead of the knee — work distally to proximally for best effect. Skipping the inner and outer quad — rotate the leg to hit all four quad heads. Doing it while watching TV and not paying attention — mindful rolling finds the real issues.
foam-roll-quads.progression: Progress: Single-leg roll with the other leg crossed on top — doubles the pressure. | Regress: Roller on a softer surface (carpet) or softer foam roller for sensitive tissue.

foam-roll-thoracic-spine.name: Foam Roll — Thoracic Spine
foam-roll-thoracic-spine.execution: Place the foam roller horizontally across your mid-back (T4-T8 level — between shoulder blades). Support your head with both hands behind the neck. Feet flat on the floor, knees bent. Allow your upper back to extend OVER the roller — let gravity do the work. Hold for 5 deep breaths, then shift the roller up 2-3 cm and repeat. Work from the mid-back up to just below the neck. Never roll the lower back.
foam-roll-thoracic-spine.why: Thoracic spine stiffness is epidemic in hockey players — the constant forward-flexed stick position for 60+ minutes per game fuses the T-spine into a rounded, kyphotic posture. A stiff T-spine forces the lumbar spine to compensate during rotation, which is a primary cause of lower-back pain and reduced shot power. 2 minutes of thoracic foam rolling unlocks the rotation that shot power requires.
foam-roll-thoracic-spine.transfer: Opens the upper back — improves shooting posture and shoulder health. Daily 60-second drill. Improves overhead position, shot rotation, and posture in one shot.
foam-roll-thoracic-spine.cues: "Roller under mid-back" · "Hands behind head" · "Drape back over roller" · "Work up the spine"
foam-roll-thoracic-spine.mistakes: Rolling the lower back — the lumbar spine should NOT be rolled. Thoracic only. Not letting the back extend — this requires you to actually relax over the roller. Moving too quickly — each segment needs 4-5 breaths of extension time. Skipping it pre-session — this is the most impactful mobility drill for shot power.
foam-roll-thoracic-spine.progression: Progress: T-spine rotation on the roller (arms crossed, rotate side to side over the roller). | Regress: Seated thoracic extension over a chair back — less intense version for very stiff T-spines.

joint-circles-full-body.name: Joint Circles — Full Body
joint-circles-full-body.execution: Start at the ankles: 10 circles each direction, each foot. Knees: 10 circles each direction with hands on knees. Hips: 10 large circles each direction — hands on hips. Shoulders: 10 arm circles forward and back. Wrists: 10 circles each direction. Neck: slow 5 circles each direction — NEVER fast neck circles.
joint-circles-full-body.why: Full-body joint circles systematically lubricate every major synovial joint with fresh synovial fluid — the joint's natural lubricant that is only distributed through movement. Cold synovial joints have less fluid coverage, move less smoothly, and are more vulnerable to impact injury. For hockey players who take hits, stop hard, and load joints in extreme positions, joint preparation is essential before every session.
joint-circles-full-body.transfer: Circulates synovial fluid in joints — reduces post-game stiffness. Pair with dynamic stretching for full warm-up sequence. Joint prep first, muscle prep second.
joint-circles-full-body.cues: "Rotate each joint through full circle both directions — ankle" · "Knee" · "Hip" · "Shoulder" · "Wrist"
joint-circles-full-body.mistakes: Rushing through it in 30 seconds — each joint needs 10 full circles. Take 2-3 minutes. Fast neck circles — the cervical spine needs slow, controlled movement only. Skipping it entirely — joint prep requires movement, not just static stretching. Only doing the joints that feel fine — the stiff joints need the circles most.
joint-circles-full-body.progression: Progress: Add loaded circles (light dumbbell for shoulder circles) once basic range is established. | Regress: Passive range (use a hand to move the joint) if active circles are restricted.
joint-circles-full-body.nameHint: Круговые вращения в суставах — всё тело

kneeling-hip-flexor-stretch.name: Kneeling Hip Flexor Stretch
kneeling-hip-flexor-stretch.execution: Kneel on one knee — back knee on the ground, front foot flat on the floor. Both hips pointing squarely forward. Tuck the pelvis under slightly (posterior pelvic tilt) — squeeze the glute of the back leg. Shift your body forward until you feel a stretch in the front of the hip of the back leg. Hold breathing into the stretch for the time prescribed on the workout card. Switch sides. Both hip flexors, every session.
kneeling-hip-flexor-stretch.why: The kneeling hip flexor stretch is the most accessible and effective stretch for the iliopsoas — the deep hip flexor that pulls the lumbar spine into anterior tilt when tight. In hockey players, a tight iliopsoas from hours of skating crouch compresses the lumbar facet joints, inhibits glute firing, and reduces stride length. Daily stretching of this muscle is one of the fastest ways to improve skating mechanics.
kneeling-hip-flexor-stretch.transfer: Counteracts the chronic hip flexor tightness from skating — reduces back pain. If your skating stride is choppy, your hip flexors are tight. This is the cheapest fix.
kneeling-hip-flexor-stretch.cues: "Rear knee on ground" · "Drive hips forward" · "Squeeze rear glute" · "Hold for the time prescribed on the workout card."
kneeling-hip-flexor-stretch.mistakes: Not tucking the pelvis — without this, you're not actually stretching the iliopsoas. Front knee going past the toes — shift it back so the shin is vertical. Cutting the hold short — the iliopsoas needs real time under tension to release. Skipping it post-skate when the hip flexors are pumped — that's the most important time.
kneeling-hip-flexor-stretch.progression: Progress: Elevated rear foot hip flexor stretch (couch stretch) — significantly deeper stretch. | Regress: Standing hip flexor stretch (one foot forward, lean back slightly) — less range required.

lat-overhead-stretch.name: Lat Overhead Stretch
lat-overhead-stretch.execution: Kneel facing a bench or box. Place both elbows on the surface, shoulder-width. Hips are over the knees. Hands can grip each other or the surface. Let the chest sink TOWARD the floor — the lats stretch as the arms go overhead. Hold breathing into the stretch for the time prescribed on the workout card. For a unilateral version: one arm on the surface, reach the other overhead and lean away. Both stretches are valuable — do both.
lat-overhead-stretch.why: The lats are chronically tight in hockey players from all the pulling, checking, and hunched posture over the stick. Tight lats internally rotate the shoulder (worsening impingement risk), limit overhead range, and pull the thoracic spine into flexion. Overhead lat stretching is essential before any overhead pressing and as daily maintenance for shoulder health and T-spine posture.
lat-overhead-stretch.transfer: Releases the lats after pull-ups and rows — improves overhead shoulder mobility. Useful pre-AND-post overhead lifting. Lat prep makes the press cleaner; lat recovery prevents next-day stiffness.
lat-overhead-stretch.cues: "Reach one arm overhead" · "Lean to the opposite side. Hold. Other side. Keep ribs down."
lat-overhead-stretch.mistakes: Hips not over the knees — moving the hips back reduces the lat stretch. Arching the lower back to get lower — the movement should come from the thoracic spine. Holding for only 10-15 seconds — lats need 30+ seconds to release meaningfully. Only doing it before pressing — lats should be stretched daily.
lat-overhead-stretch.progression: Progress: Active lat stretch with a dowel overhead — adds a mobility control component. | Regress: Standing doorway lat stretch (one arm gripping the frame, leaning away) — easier position.',
lat-overhead-stretch.muscles: Latissimus Dorsi, Teres Major, Thoracic Spine

overhead-tricep-stretch.name: Overhead Tricep Stretch
overhead-tricep-stretch.execution: Raise one arm straight up overhead. Bend the elbow — let the forearm drop behind the head. Use the opposite hand to gently pull the elbow further behind the head. Hold for the time prescribed on the workout card. Feel the stretch along the back of the upper arm and shoulder. Switch sides. Keep the torso upright — don't lean to one side.
overhead-tricep-stretch.why: The overhead tricep stretch lengthens the long head of the triceps — which crosses the shoulder joint and becomes chronically tight in hockey players from the constant elbow-bent shooting and stick-handling position. Tight tricep long heads restrict overhead range and contribute to the shoulder impingement pattern. Two sets daily helps maintain the overhead mobility needed for safe pressing and physical play with arms raised.
overhead-tricep-stretch.transfer: Releases triceps after pressing — prevents elbow and shoulder tightness. Pair with thoracic rotation drills. Tricep + T-spine = overhead position fully restored.
overhead-tricep-stretch.cues: "Raise one arm overhead" · "Bend elbow behind head" · "Use other hand to gently push down. Hold."
overhead-tricep-stretch.mistakes: Pulling too aggressively — gentle sustained pressure only. Leaning the torso sideways — stay upright. Only 15-20 second holds — minimum 30 seconds for tissue change. Forgetting the shooting arm — dominant side typically tighter.
overhead-tricep-stretch.progression: Progress: Add a gentle lateral lean away from the raised arm — increases stretch intensity. | Regress: Door frame tricep stretch (elbow on frame, lean forward) — passive version.

pancake-stretch.name: Pancake Stretch
pancake-stretch.execution: Sit on the floor with legs spread as wide as comfortable — gradually increase over weeks. Sit tall on the sitting bones — don't let the pelvis tuck under. Hinge FORWARD at the hips — chest moves toward the floor, not the forehead. Walk hands forward along the floor as you descend. Hold the deepest position for 30-60 seconds, breathing into the hips. Add active rotations: turn the torso to face each leg and hold.
pancake-stretch.why: The pancake stretch (seated wide-leg forward fold) targets the hip adductors, hamstrings, and hip external rotators in their most lengthened position — creating the extreme hip mobility required for goalie splits, wide defensive stances, and the maximum stride width of an explosive skating push-off. Regular pancake work directly increases stride width, which is one of the largest biomechanical contributors to skating speed.
pancake-stretch.transfer: Extreme groin and hamstring flexibility — critical for goalies and tight turns. Daily work, but be patient. Pancake gains come over months, not weeks. The investment compounds.
pancake-stretch.cues: "Seated wide legs" · "Rotate chest toward one leg" · "Then center" · "Then other side"
pancake-stretch.mistakes: Rounding the lower back to reach further — hinge at the hip, keep the spine long. Legs not wide enough — the stretch must feel challenging. Add width over weeks. Only holding passively — add active movements (torso rotations) for more mobility transfer. Forcing it — adductor tears happen when aggressive stretching meets cold tissue. Warm up first.
pancake-stretch.progression: Progress: Weighted pancake — plate on the back increases gravity assist into the fold. | Regress: Butterfly stretch — same adductor target with less range requirement.

scorpion-stretch.name: Scorpion Stretch
scorpion-stretch.execution: Lie face down, arms extended out to the sides in a T-position. Lift the right foot and swing it across the body toward the left hand — like a scorpion tail. Try to touch the left hand with the right foot without the right shoulder leaving the floor. Hold the end position 2-3 seconds. Feel the stretch across the hip, groin, and T-spine. Return and switch sides — left foot swings to the right hand. 8-10 reps each side as a dynamic warm-up.
scorpion-stretch.why: The scorpion stretch mobilises the thoracic spine, hip flexors, and posterior hip simultaneously in a rotational pattern — making it one of the highest-efficiency mobility drills available. For hockey players, this combined thoracic + hip mobility is what's required for powerful rotational shots and the full hip extension at the end of a skating stride. It also counteracts the chronic posterior hip tightness from skating.
scorpion-stretch.transfer: Dynamic spinal rotation and hip mobility — great pre-skate activation. If you can't keep both shoulders down while swinging the leg over, that's the data. Work the limited side more.
scorpion-stretch.cues: "Lie face down" · "Reach foot to opposite hand behind you" · "Let hip rotate"
scorpion-stretch.mistakes: Shoulder lifting off the floor — keep both shoulders grounded. Forcing range — the foot doesn't need to touch the hand. Stretch, don't crank. Rushing through it — hold the end position 2-3 seconds for mobility benefit. Skipping it pre-session — 2 minutes of scorpions unlocks more mobility than 10 minutes of static stretches.
scorpion-stretch.progression: Progress: Add a pause and active reach at the end position — turns it into a mobility strengthening drill. | Regress: Supine figure-4 with gentle pull — same hip target with no T-spine demand.
scorpion-stretch.muscles: Hip Flexors, Thoracic Spine, Glutes, Adductors

seated-hamstring-stretch.name: Seated Hamstring Stretch
seated-hamstring-stretch.execution: Sit on the floor with one leg extended, the other foot against the inner thigh. Sit tall on both sitting bones — don't let the lower back round. Hinge FORWARD from the hips — chest moves toward the thigh, not the forehead toward the knee. Reach for the foot or ankle — or use a strap around the foot. Hold breathing steadily for the time prescribed on the workout card. With each exhale, inch forward slightly. Switch sides. Both hamstrings, both sessions.
seated-hamstring-stretch.why: Hamstring flexibility directly affects skating stride length — tight hamstrings limit hip extension at the back of the stride, reducing stride length and top-end skating speed. Research shows hockey players have measurably shorter strides than their potential maximum due to hamstring restriction. Regular seated hamstring stretching, held for 60+ seconds, progressively restores the range needed for full stride expression.
seated-hamstring-stretch.transfer: Lengthens the hamstrings after deadlifts and speed work — prevents lower back pain. Pair with hinge work (RDL, single-leg RDL). Stretch length + load strength = bulletproof posterior chain.
seated-hamstring-stretch.cues: "Sit with legs straight" · "Hinge forward from hips (not rounding spine)" · "Reach toward feet. Hold."
seated-hamstring-stretch.mistakes: Rounding the lower back to reach further — hinge at the hip. The stretch is in the hamstring, not the spine. Holding only 20-30 seconds — minimum 45 seconds for neurological release. Pulling the toes toward the shin while stretching — adds nerve tension. Relax the foot. Skipping post-skate — warm hamstrings are 40% more responsive to stretching.
seated-hamstring-stretch.progression: Progress: Standing hamstring stretch with foot elevated — more range and a different neural demand. | Regress: Supine hamstring stretch (band around foot, leg raised) — gravity-assisted, easier on the hips.

standing-quad-stretch.name: Standing Quad Stretch
standing-quad-stretch.execution: Stand on one leg. Grip the opposite ankle with the same-side hand. Pull the heel toward the glute — feel the stretch at the front of the thigh. Keep the knees together — the stretching knee should not drift to the side. Stand tall — don't lean forward. Squeeze the glute of the stretching leg. Hold for the time prescribed on the workout card. Switch sides. Use a wall for balance if needed.
standing-quad-stretch.why: The standing quad stretch targets the rectus femoris — the quad head that crosses both the hip and knee — which becomes chronically shortened from the constant skating crouch. A tight rectus femoris pulls the pelvis into anterior tilt, compressing the lumbar spine and inhibiting glute activation. Regular stretching restores hip extension range and immediately improves skating stride length at the back of the push-off.
standing-quad-stretch.transfer: Releases the quads after heavy lower body work — critical for knee health. If standing balance is an issue, hold a wall. The stretch matters more than the balance practice on this one.
standing-quad-stretch.cues: "Stand on one leg" · "Pull heel to glute" · "Keep knees together" · "Stand tall. Balance or hold wall."
standing-quad-stretch.mistakes: Knee drifting out to the side — keep knees together throughout. Leaning the torso forward — stay upright. The stretch comes from the hip, not the torso. Only 20-30 second holds — the rectus femoris needs 45+ seconds. Not squeezing the glute — the glute squeeze enhances the hip flexor stretch.
standing-quad-stretch.progression: Progress: Couch stretch — significantly deeper rectus femoris stretch. | Regress: Lying quad stretch (lie on side, pull heel toward glute) — for those with poor balance.
